description.en:
An ontology for representing historical place knowledge as attestations:
        bundles of evidence linking SpatialEntities (settlements, routes,
        networks, administrative units, regions and other entities whose
        identity is bound up with space) to Names, Geometries, Timespans,
        Types, PropertyValues and Authorities with full provenance.

        Developed by the Pelagios Network's Place Working Group, led by the
        Institute for Spatial History Innovation (ISHI), University of Pittsburgh.

        PLATO formalises the WHG v4 data model, in which the Attestation is
        the fundamental unit of contributed knowledge. The Linked Places
        Format (LPF) is defined as its single-object-attestation profile:
        every LPF element corresponds to one attestation linking one entity
        to one name, type, geometry or related entity, so existing LPF files
        remain valid. The use cases of Linked Traces are accommodated within
        the same model.

bibliographicCitation.value: Gadd, Stephen, and the Pelagios Network Place Working Group. PLATO — Place Attestation Ontology, version 0.8.0. Zenodo, 2026. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21688313

comment.en:
A spatial representation of a SpatialEntity's extent or location. Geometries
        are independent, reusable entities. The same Geometry may be referenced
        by multiple Attestations across different SpatialEntities or time periods.

        Each Geometry is one GeoJSON geometry; a GeometryCollection is not
        accepted, so a set of different kinds (a point and a polygon) is
        several Geometry nodes. One attestation may attest several
        geometries when one source gives them all, each with a
        plato:geometry_role where they depict different things (a built
        extent, a label position); a geometry from another source is
        another attestation, since it has another provenance. See
        examples/geometry-roles.ttl.

        A geometry traced from a historical map, and placed in the world
        through a georeference (a IIIF Georeference Annotation, such as one
        made in Allmaps), is evidence of what the map shows, so it is
        attested, not plato:computed. Its position depends on the map, on the
        annotation, whose control points can be edited after the tracing,
        and on the transformation fitted to them. So the attestation cites
        both, and no new property is needed: the map as the evidence
        (plato:citation_function cito:citesAsEvidence), with the canvas as
        the plato:locator, and '#xywh=' added when the tracing is from a
        region of it; and the annotation as a Source of its own, with the
        annotation's IRI, plato:derived_from the map's Source, cited with
        cito:usesMethodIn. The transformation (polynomial of order 1 to 3,
        thin plate spline, projective, Helmert) and the number of control
        points used go in the attestation's plato:notes, since the annotation
        may since have changed. A position that is where the map writes a
        name takes plato:geometry_role plato:LabelAnchor. The position of a
        map symbol is a plato:RepresentativePoint, unless the map shows the
        specific feature (a church drawn as such), when it is a
        plato:FeaturePoint. See
        schemas/examples/place-centric-georeference.json.

A toponym or appellation for a SpatialEntity. Names are independent, reusable
        entities. The association between a Name and a SpatialEntity is always mediated
        by an Attestation, which provides temporal scope and provenance.

One attestation's use of one Authority: the qualified form of
        plato:sourced_by. Carries what is true of this citation rather than
        of the source or of the attestation: the locator within the work
        (page, folio, column, table cell, entry), and whether the attribution
        was stated in the source or inferred editorially. It carries no date.
        The date of a witness belongs on the Source (plato:source_timespan)
        and the date of the claim on the Attestation's Timespan.

        An attestation resting on several sources has several Citations,
        each with its own locator. Where there is nothing to say about the
        citation, plato:sourced_by alone is sufficient.

An assertion that two SpatialEntities refer to the same real-world entity.
        Carries its own provenance (who asserted it, on what basis),
        certainty (how confident the assertion is), and identity semantics
        (exactMatch, closeMatch, related).

        Identity relations are distinct from scholarly entity-to-entity
        relations, which describe substantive historical relationships
        between different entities. They are also distinct from Candidates,
        which are matches suggested by software and are claims by no one; a
        relation made in answer to one points to it (plato:promoted_from).

        An IdentityRelation is one attributed claim among many, never a
        canonical statement of fact. A platform must not materialise identity
        relations into merged records or minted identifiers, nor let one
        outweigh contrary evidence by fiat: it is weighed like any other
        evidence, and someone else may say the opposite (an attestation with
        plato:negated bundling an exactMatch says two entities are not the
        same).

        Identity relations asserted together, as when a person accepts a
        cluster of matches, are bundled by one Attestation
        (plato:attests_identity), which carries their shared provenance and
        is withdrawn or amended as a unit. A consumer may take the transitive
        closure of exactMatch relations within one such attestation, and must
        not chain identity relations across different attestations, nor
        chain closeMatch, related or unspecified ones at all: A the same as B
        and B the same as C, asserted by different people, is not anyone's
        assertion that A is C.

A mutable, versioned workspace of SpatialEntities and Attestations,
        owned by a contributor or team. Replaces the WHG v3
        concepts of Dataset, Dataset Collection, and Place Collection.
        A Gazetteer can be incrementally edited, enriched, and corrected
        without re-ingestion.

        A Gazetteer's attestations need not be about SpatialEntities it
        defines. It may attest evidence about SpatialEntities defined in other
        Gazetteers, identified by their IRIs, without redefining them: a
        correction to another project's place, a link from a record to an
        existing place, a curator's selection of places for a collection.
        Such an attestation adds evidence. It does not change the entity's
        identity or make this Gazetteer its owner, and its source, contributor
        and status are this Gazetteer's. The append-only rule of a published
        Gazetteer applies to the attestations it contains, not to everything
        said elsewhere about its entities. In PLATO JSON such attestations go
        in an attestation-centric document, whose 'about' gives the entity's
        IRI; a place-centric document declares every SpatialEntity it lists
        (plato:contains_entity), so it lists only its own.

        As a dcat:Dataset, a Gazetteer is titled with dcterms:title and
        licensed with dcterms:license. Not with plato:authority_title or
        plato:licence: their domains are plato:Authority and plato:Dataset,
        so using them would make the Gazetteer one of the Authorities it
        contains attestations about.

        Described for discovery and citation (the FAIR principles), again in
        the vocabularies a catalogue already reads: dcterms:creator for the
        people to cite (plato:gazetteer_owner, its owner, is not necessarily
        an author); dcat:keyword; dcterms:spatial for the area it covers, as
        an address; dcterms:temporal for the years it covers, a
        dcterms:PeriodOfTime with dcat:startDate and dcat:endDate;
        dcat:landingPage; and void:uriSpace, the base from which its entities'
        IRIs are made. A published Gazetteer (plato:gazetteer_status
        'published') must state its dcterms:license: data others are to reuse
        needs its terms stated. All the other descriptive properties are
        optional.

        Versions, and so citations that reproduce. A SpatialEntity's evidence
        grows and is corrected while its identity stays the same, so a
        citation of it must say which state was meant. For the same reason
        as above, a Gazetteer's version uses DCAT 3's own properties, not a
        PLATO one: dcat:version for its version indicator, and, for a frozen
        snapshot published under its own IRI, dcat:isVersionOf (the living
        Gazetteer) and dcat:previousVersion (the snapshot before). A
        SpatialEntity is then cited as its IRI plus the Gazetteer version,
        one number per gazetteer rather than one per entity, as PeriodO cites.

        Once a Gazetteer's plato:gazetteer_status is 'published', its
        attestations are append-only, and this is normative: an attestation is
        never deleted or changed. What an attestation says includes its
        facets and citations (plato:attests_name, attests_geometry,
        attests_timespan, attests_type, attests_property, attests_identity,
        plato:has_citation) whether or not they have IRIs of their own: a Name
        shared under its IRI is not re-spelt once published, since that would
        change every attestation pointing to it. The SpatialEntities and
        Authorities that attestations are about or cite are not attestations,
        and their descriptions may still be corrected and enriched. Every
        attestation in a published Gazetteer should have a permanent IRI of
        its own, since a correction or withdrawal must point to its target;
        this is a recommendation, meant to become a requirement. A correction
        is a new attestation with a meta-attestation (plato:Supersedes,
        plato:Contradicts), and a
        withdrawal is a meta-attestation of type plato:Retracts. Each carries
        plato:created. The state as of any moment D is then a filter over the
        data: the attestations created by D, less those superseded or
        retracted by D. A supersession or retraction takes effect only while
        it holds itself, so retracting a retraction restores its target, and
        a chain of them resolves the same way; a cycle is an error in the
        data. A platform can offer that state on request, by
        datetime negotiation on the entity's IRI (RFC 7089, Memento); PLATO
        recommends this but does not require it, since it is behaviour of a
        server, not of data.

A person, team, or automated process that creates attestations.
        Aligned with both foaf:Agent and prov:Agent for provenance
        chain-of-custody tracking.

        Contributors should be identified using persistent identifiers where
        possible. For persons, ORCID (https://orcid.org/) is strongly
        recommended and may be required by specific implementations. ORCID
        identifiers should use the full URI format (https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000)
        rather than just the numeric portion, as ORCID is particular about
        proper URI formatting for linked data interoperability.

        For organizations, ROR (https://ror.org/) or ISNI identifiers are
        recommended. Proper identification ensures accurate attribution,
        enables citation, and supports research assessment.
The subject is where the target person was born.

The subject is a member of the target route, itinerary or network: a
        station on a road, a stop on a journey, a port in a trade network, a
        segment of a river system. Its position, where the source gives one,
        is plato:sequence on the same attestation. A route may be a member of
        another route (one stage of a pilgrimage), but not, through any chain
        of memberships, of itself. Not containment: a town on a road is not
        within it, and a network's members need not lie inside anything.

The subject SpatialEntity is contained in the target SpatialEntity, for
        the attested timespan: a parish in a hundred, a hundred in a county.
        Not an identity relation and not fixed by the class model; it is a
        claim, with a source and a certainty, like any other attestation.

        When a dataset's containing regions are matched to a gazetteer (a
        parish's county and country, looked up level by level), two claims
        are made, and kept apart. The dataset's own claim is ContainedIn,
        pointing at a region minted from the dataset itself, one for each
        full chain of containers (England, Surrey), never for the name
        alone, so that two regions with one name in different chains are not
        merged. The reviewer's decision that this region is the gazetteer's is
        an IdentityRelation from it, whose promoted_from names the Candidate
        that holds the matching software's similarity_score. A match score is
        not a certainty, so it is never put on the containment. In Linked
        Places Format the two are written together as one
        gvp:broaderPartitive relation: its relationTo is the identity's
        object, its certainty the identity attestation's certainty level, its
        whg_match_score the Candidate's score and its label the region's
        name. A region assigned by hand, with no software suggestion, may be
        stated directly against the gazetteer's address instead.
The subject is where the target person died.

The target is about the subject: an archival file, a site record, a report or a publication, identified by its address. Not a citation of the target as evidence for another statement, which is plato:has_citation.

The subject is land that the target people lived in or held, as the source says: the target is a people described elsewhere, identified by its address where it has one, and named by plato:related_label. A people is not itself a SpatialEntity.

The subject and target are directly connected, in no particular
        direction: an attestation that A is connected to B says the same as
        one that B is connected to A. For a connection that runs one way, use
        plato:LeadsTo. A connection known in both directions from sources that
        each give one is better recorded as two LeadsTo attestations, each
        with its own source, than as one ConnectedTo.
The target person or group lived at the subject, for the attested timespan.
The target person or group worked, or held office, at the subject, for the attested timespan: Linked Traces' heldOffice, and work generally.
The subject is shown in the target: a photograph, map, plan, drawing or other image, identified by its address in a collection.

A directed connection, from the subject (attests_about) to the target
        (relates_to): one river flowing into another, a post road carrying
        mail from one town to the next, letters sent from one city to
        another. It joins two places; the reaches and legs of a network are
        segments, whose direction is given by plato:BeginsAt and
        plato:EndsAt. Not river-specific: a project declares its own narrower types ('flows
        into', 'carries post to') with plato:broader_relation pointing here,
        so that a consumer that knows only LeadsTo still follows them in the
        right direction.

The subject segment begins at the target: a leg of an itinerary at the
        station it leaves, a river reach at its upstream confluence. With
        plato:EndsAt it gives a segment a direction. A segment with no
        direction is joined to its two ends with plato:HasEnd.
The target event (a battle, a council, a fair) took place at the subject, wholly or in part.
The target object (a coin, an inscription, a manuscript) was found at the subject. The timespan is when it was found, if known.

The subject segment ends at the target: a leg of an itinerary at the
        station it reaches, a river reach at its downstream confluence. See
        plato:BeginsAt.

The subject segment has the target as one of its ends, in no
        particular direction: a stretch of road between two towns, walked
        either way. An undirected segment has two HasEnd attestations. Not
        plato:ConnectedTo, which joins two places directly: were a segment
        connected to its ends, every place would be two steps from its
        neighbours.

A vocabulary entry defining a semantic relationship between SpatialEntities:
        'capital_of', 'successor_to', 'connected_by_trade_route_to', etc.
        Carries a label, an inverse label, and domain/range constraints.
        This allows the vocabulary of historical relationships to grow
        without modifying the core ontology.

An organization to which a Contributor is affiliated. This is a
        lightweight class defined primarily to avoid ambiguity in ontology
        visualizations. Organizations can be further described using properties
        from FOAF, schema.org, or other ontologies.

        Organizations should use persistent identifiers where possible:
        - ROR (Research Organization Registry): https://ror.org/
        - ISNI (International Standard Name Identifier)
        - Wikidata QIDs
Starter concepts for plato:occurrence_context. The capacity in which an attested form occurs in its source.
Starter concepts for plato:relative_qualifier. How a facet is defined relative to its anchor when bearing and distance are not applicable or not sufficient.
Starter concepts for plato:timespan_role. What an attestation's timespans date: when what it records held, or the span of the evidence for it.
Starter concepts for plato:transcription_accuracy. How faithfully a transcribed value renders what the source shows.
Starter concepts for plato:has_meta_type. The nature of a meta-attestation's relationship to its target attestation.
Starter concepts for plato:geometry_role. What a geometry depicts, as distinct from how precisely it is known.
Starter concepts for plato:attribution_status. Whether the attribution of evidence to a cited source was stated or resolved editorially.
Starter concepts for plato:source_stance. How firmly the source itself asserts what an attestation records, as distinct from anyone's confidence in it.
Starter concepts for the kinds of SpatialEntity a platform treats specially: routes, itineraries, networks and segments. A Type attestation names one in its type identifier.
Starter concepts for plato:transcription_completeness. Whether a transcribed value is whole, and if not, whether the lost part can be supplied.
Starter concepts for plato:form_status. The status of the name form an attestation contributes.

A collection-level authority: a published gazetteer, a contributed
        dataset, or an external authority corpus (GeoNames, Wikidata, TGN,
        OSM, Pleiades). Carries metadata such as title, version, publisher,
        and URI, and a licence (dcterms:license, as for any Authority).

An entity whose identity is bound up with space, whether its spatial
        extent is attested directly, applies notionally (as with the region to
        which a period applies), or is derived from its constituents (as with a
        route or a network, whose extent is that of its members). A
        SpatialEntity need not have any attested geometry: lost, imagined and
        unlocated entities are admissible.

        A curated selection of other places, such as a thematic collection, is
        not a SpatialEntity: it is a Gazetteer, whose attestations are about
        the places it selects.

        What kind of entity it is (settlement, route, region, administrative
        unit and so on) is not fixed by the class. It is established by
        Type attestations, so a classification is a claim rather than an axiom.

        SpatialEntities are not defined by any single attestation. They are the
        point of convergence for many attestations from different sources,
        periods and contributors.

        PLATO defines no Place class and gives "place" no prescribed
        meaning. Many SpatialEntities are what people would call places and
        some are not, and the word is used differently across languages and
        disciplines. The ontology therefore neither equates a SpatialEntity
        with a place nor defines a place in terms of SpatialEntities or
        their attestations. Where the word appears in this document it is
        used in its ordinary sense.

A classification or category for a SpatialEntity, typically drawn from a
        controlled vocabulary such as the Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus
        (AAT), as one dataset uses it. A Type node stands for that usage and
        may be reused within its dataset. Its IRI, if it has one, is the
        dataset's own, or it is a blank node: never the vocabulary concept's
        IRI, which goes in plato:type_identifier. Otherwise every dataset's
        label, source wording and plato:scheme_version would merge onto the
        concept in any combined graph.

A match between two SpatialEntities suggested by software, for a person
        to review: reconciliation against reference gazetteers (as in WHG's Map
        your Data), record linkage, clustering. A Candidate carries a similarity
        score, the algorithm's version, optionally the settings that produced
        the score (plato:match_parameters), when it was generated, and the status
        it had when its CandidateSet was issued, 'suggested'. It is a
        claim by no one, and never becomes an IdentityRelation: a reviewer's
        answer is an Attestation bundling an IdentityRelation that points back
        through plato:promoted_from, a match or, with plato:negated, a denial.

        A Candidate is published only in a CandidateSet, and is frozen from then
        on, like a published attestation: never changed, never deleted, so that
        a promoted_from pointing at it keeps its meaning. What became of it is
        therefore derived, not stored. Take the attestations as of a moment
        (those created by then, less those retracted or superseded; see
        plato:Gazetteer) whose identity relations point at the Candidate: it is
        accepted where some are and none is negated, rejected where some are
        negated and none is not, answered both ways where there are both, and
        unanswered where there are none. Identity is attributed, so a consumer
        may ask this of one reviewer's or one gazetteer's attestations only.

        Its IRI is a fragment of the IRI of the CandidateSet that publishes it,
        minted from what it says: the set's IRI without any fragment, then '#c-'
        and the first 8 hex digits (lower case) of the SHA-256 of a JSON array of
        four strings, the source's IRI, the candidate's IRI, the algorithm
        version and the match parameters (empty when there are none), written in
        the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (RFC 8785) and hashed as UTF-8 with no
        Unicode normalisation. Where 8 digits would begin like another
        Candidate's hash, in its set or in an earlier set given to the minter,
        it takes the shortest prefix, in steps of 4 digits, that differs from
        every other. An IRI once published is never changed. A later set leaves
        out a Candidate an earlier set already published, so each Candidate has
        one IRI, under the set that first published it. The time it was
        generated is not hashed. '#a-' is the form of an attestation's IRI,
        never a Candidate's.

definition.value: A form derived from an attested one for matching or search, attested by no source and carrying no independent evidential value.
The span of the evidence: the dates of the earliest and latest documents that mention the entity. Not the dates of the entity itself.
A set of places and the connections between them, in no single order: a river system, a canal network, a correspondence network.
The form survives only as an element of a later minor name, such as a field name.
On the far side of the anchor from the point of view of the source.
A proxy point standing in for the whole SpatialEntity, for indexing and display; it need not depict any feature of it.
The built or bounded extent of the SpatialEntity.
The location of a specific central feature of the SpatialEntity, such as a market place or a church.
The period during which what the attestation records held, according to the source. The default.
Part of the value is lost, damaged or abbreviated, but can be supplied with confidence.
The source is named where the form occurs. The default attribution status, usually omitted.

This attestation and the target are alternative readings of the same evidence: at most one of them is right. Each keeps its own certainty. Link every alternative in a set to the same first one. A set of alternatives is one piece of evidence, not several, so it must be counted once.
The editorial or preferred form under which the cited authority files the entry. A scholarly decision rather than a reading.
The source was given as ibidem or idem and resolved by an editor, so the attribution is inferred rather than stated.
The source raises it and declines to settle it. Not a denial, which is plato:negated.
Asserts that the target attestation is incorrect.
Inside the anchor.
The transcription renders what the source shows.

The target attestation is withdrawn: it no longer holds, and is kept only so that earlier states of the gazetteer can be reproduced. For a claim its maker takes back, such as a bad import, where plato:Contradicts would read as one scholar disputing another. A tool showing the current state leaves a retracted attestation out. A retraction is itself an attestation: retracting it withdraws the withdrawal, and the target holds again.
Adds a remark about the target attestation, with its own source, without supporting, contradicting or refining it. The remark is the meta-attestation's notes.
The source states it, but with a hedge: 'as it seems', 'were (if not are)'.
The form refers to the SpatialEntity directly. The default occurrence context, usually omitted.
Questions the validity of the target attestation.
A form written by the editors of the cited edition in their own words (commentary, apparatus, notes), not a form the edited source itself contains.

scopeNote.value: Use it when the citation is to an edition and the name occurs in the editors' text, not in the edited text. It says nothing about whether the place's name is attested elsewhere. Attested remains the default for forms the source contains.

definition.value: The form the contributing project prefers for display and search: a project decision, so the cited source may show a different form.
Replaces the target attestation with newer information.
A physical link with an existence of its own: a leg of a route between two stations, a reach of a river between confluences. Platforms may leave segments out of lists and searches of places.
A form read in the cited source. The default form status, usually omitted.
A timespan defined by the reign or tenure of the anchor.
The transcribed form is not in the source at all: a ghost form, kept because it circulates and must be recognisable.
The source passes it on without vouching for it: 'it is said', 'as Cambden noteth'.
The anchor point of a map label.
This attestation's value was derived from the target attestation's, as a normalised search form is derived from an attested spelling.
A line tracing a route or journey.
The source states it as so, on its own account. The default source stance, usually omitted.
A form inferred but not attested; the philologists' asterisked form.
Close to the anchor, without a stated bearing or distance.
Provides more precise information than the target attestation.
Between two anchors, given as two values of plato:relative_to, in no particular order.
A name defined as a variant of the anchor name.
Nothing of the value is lost.
Provides additional evidence for the target attestation.
An ordered set of places making a way: a road, a sea lane, a pilgrimage route. Its timespan, if any, is when it was in use, not when anyone travelled it.
The form occurs only as an element of a personal name, a surname or by-name; the (p) of the place-name surveys.
Part of the value is lost and cannot be supplied.
The transcription departs from what the source shows, by misreading or error, but is a reading of something the source contains.

A journey made through places in order, each stop with its own timespan: a traveller's tour, a royal progress, a ship's voyage. Not plato:Itinerary, which is a geometry role (a line tracing a route or journey).
Groups the target with other related attestations.
Upstream of the anchor along a watercourse.

comment.en:
Abstract superclass for all reference entities that provide provenance
        or semantic grounding for attestations. Subtypes include Source,
        Dataset, Period, RelationType, and CertaintyLevel.
The statement is certain: the source, or the contributor, has no doubt of it.
The statement is probable but not certain.
The statement is doubtful: possible, but not established.

A defined level of certainty for use in attestations, allowing
        projects to standardise their confidence vocabulary. An attestation or
        facet points at one with plato:certainty_level. PLATO declares the three
        levels of Linked Places Format (plato:Certain, plato:LessCertain,
        plato:Uncertain); a project may declare its own.

A quantitative or descriptive attribute of a SpatialEntity, expressed as a
        property drawn from an external vocabulary together with its value.
        Covers the many things a historical source says that are neither a
        name, a location, a period nor a classification — populations,
        valuations, elevations, recurrence rules for markets and fairs.

        The property itself is identified by URI rather than enumerated here,
        so the vocabulary stays open and delegated (Wikidata properties,
        CIDOC-CRM, project vocabularies), in the same way that Type delegates
        its classifications to AAT.

        Values may be literals (with a datatype and optional unit) or
        structured objects whose shape is declared by plato:value_type. As a
        facet node, a PropertyValue may carry the qualification properties
        (certainty, fuzziness) like any other.

        Where the value is another SpatialEntity, use an entity-to-entity
        relation instead; this class is for attributes of the entity. A person
        or organisation connected to it (the grantee of a market right, an
        owner, a lord of the manor) is such an attribute: the value is the
        agent's IRI, ideally in an authority such as Wikidata or VIAF, with
        value_datatype xsd:anyURI, and the property names the role, for
        example http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/P127 ('owned by'). This
        asserts nothing false, and needs no agent class: PLATO's own agent
        classes (Contributor, Organization) describe who recorded the data.

        A figure from a statistical table (a census count, a toll receipt) is
        a PropertyValue that is also a qb:Observation of the W3C RDF Data
        Cube vocabulary. It carries qb:dataSet (the table, a qb:DataSet), one
        direct statement for each of its coordinates with the table's
        qb:DimensionProperty predicates, one for each fact about the figure
        with qb:AttributeProperty predicates (sdmx-attribute:obsStatus for a
        cell's state), and plato:universe for the figure it is a part or share
        of. So the county is not said to have 'class 1': the observation is.
        The measure stays plato:property_type and plato:value_literal, and the
        area and date stay on the attestation; a cube export adds the direct
        measure statement, sdmx-dimension:refArea and refPeriod. A printed dash
        is an observation with an obsStatus and no value, never 0. Money is
        an exact integer in the smallest unit of its system of account
        (farthings, for sterling amounts with halfpennies), the unit an IRI
        from a fitting authority or minted by the encoding project, ideally
        naming a unit of account in a named system ('penny sterling'); PLATO
        mints no currency and converts nothing. A coordinate the source does
        not give is an explicit 'unknown' code. A table mixing measures is one
        qb:DataSet per measure. Dimension values are concepts, with the
        source's label as skos:prefLabel, in code lists the encoding project
        publishes where none exists. A statistical table in spreadsheet form
        keeps its own CSV on the Web description and links to places by
        place_id. The design, and its testing on three corpora, is issue #14.

        A latitude given without a longitude (a source's 'at 9.5 degrees
        north') is a PropertyValue, not a Geometry, since it is not a location:
        property http://www.w3.org/2003/01/geo/wgs84_pos#lat, the value in
        decimal degrees. A longitude alone is the same, with wgs84_pos#long.

The matches one run of matching software suggested for a dataset's
        SpatialEntities (plato:candidates_for), published together for people
        to review and for the dataset's identity relations to point at
        (plato:promoted_from). A Candidate is published only in a candidate
        set, never in a Gazetteer: a Gazetteer holds claims, and a Candidate
        is a claim by no one.

        A candidate set is issued once (dcterms:issued) and frozen from then
        on: no Candidate in it is changed or deleted, and a later run is a new
        set. A dataset whose identity relations cite a candidate set should
        have that set published wherever the dataset is, so that
        promoted_from can be followed; a validator that has the set should
        warn when a promoted_from names no Candidate in it.

        As a dcat:Dataset it is titled with dcterms:title and licensed with
        dcterms:license, as a Gazetteer is. It is disjoint from Gazetteer, so
        it carries none of a Gazetteer's own properties (a status, an owner):
        its date of issue says from when it is frozen.

A bundle of evidence asserting that a particular SpatialEntity had a particular
        Name, Geometry, Type, or combination thereof, during a particular
        Timespan, according to a particular Authority. The Attestation node
        carries only metadata; its semantic content is defined entirely by its
        outgoing relationships.

        IMPORTANT: Attestations are document nodes in the graph, not edges.
        They are instances of plato:Attestation (a class), not instances of
        owl:ObjectProperty. This design enables meta-attestations and full
        provenance tracking.

A temporal interval with start and end bounds. Timespans are
        independent, reusable entities that may be shared across multiple
        Attestations. Precision and uncertainty are expressed through
        the start and end bound properties. Aligned with W3C Time Ontology
        and compatible with PeriodO period definitions.

A citable source of evidence: a manuscript, chronicle, tax record,
        map, scholarly article, or other document. Sources are the primary
        provenance anchor for attestations. A Source may reference its parent
        Dataset via plato:partOf.

        A Source's licence, that of the edition or copy cited, is given with
        dcterms:license, as a Gazetteer's is. A project that admits evidence
        by its licence (citing a share-alike source as a witness but never
        copying it, say) needs the licence on the thing cited, so that it
        travels with the data.

A thematic or organisational grouping of Gazetteers (e.g.
        'EMEW — Gazetteer of Early Modern England and Wales').

A named historical period (e.g. 'Byzantine', 'Early Modern'),
        optionally linked to PeriodO or defined locally. Includes temporal
        bounds for period-based querying.

Human-readable label for this timespan (e.g., 'Byzantine period',
        'Early Bronze Age', 'Ming Dynasty'). Particularly useful for named
        periods referenced across multiple attestations. The date exactly as a
        source writes it ('c. 925', 'a. 1300') is plato:source_label.

The version of the vocabulary (the skos:inScheme of this Type) that the
        type was taken from: '2017' for the RESOLVE ecoregions, a release date
        for OpenStreetMap's tag definitions. Needed where a scheme's terms
        change meaning between versions; otherwise optional. JSON
        schemeVersion, tables type_scheme_version, beside the scheme (JSON
        scheme, tables type_scheme).

True when this value, or this whole attestation, was worked out by
        software from other data rather than taken from a source: an
        itinerary's timespan from the timespans of its stops, a route's
        geometry from its stations. A computed value is not evidence. A
        consumer may show it, but must not take it in as an attestation of
        its own: it should compute the value again from the members, or leave
        it out and say so. Absent or false, a value is attested.

        It is for a value derived from other statements in the same data,
        which any consumer holding them could derive again. A figure a
        project works out from its own source material and publishes as a
        finding (letters counted from a register, a median taken over them)
        is not computed in this sense: it is attested, citing the work that
        produced it as a Source or Dataset derived_from the material it was
        worked out from. Nor is a geometry traced from a map and placed
        through a georeference: software fits the transformation, but the
        geometry is evidence of what the map shows (see plato:Geometry).

        It is not plato:form_status Normalised (a name form an editor
        derived from an attested one), nor a Candidate (a match an algorithm
        suggests). Like the qualification properties it has no rdfs:domain,
        so it can mark an Attestation or any facet node.

The concept's IRI in a controlled vocabulary: an AAT, Wikidata or
        GeoNames concept, an OpenStreetMap tag. It should be a full IRI, not a
        bare code ('PPL', 'Q687188', 'stream') whose vocabulary is known only
        from somewhere else: that is what lets types from different sources be
        compared. An OpenStreetMap tag's IRI carries its key
        (https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Tag:waterway=stream), since the
        value alone is ambiguous. A source's own category that no vocabulary
        holds is recorded as the Type's label and plato:source_label, with no
        identifier, rather than as a code made up for it. The IRI is written
        as a literal typed xsd:anyURI, never as an IRI object: that is what
        the JSON-LD context and the spreadsheet tables produce, and one form
        lets queries compare identifiers without converting them.

Extended Date/Time Format (EDTF) representation of this timespan.
        Provides standardized string encoding for interchange with systems
        using EDTF. Optional but recommended for interoperability with library
        and archival systems. Example: '1453-05-29/1453-05-29' or '1450~/1453~'
        for approximate dates.

The original label as given in the contributing source, before
        vocabulary mapping. For a structured PropertyValue this preserves the
        unparsed original — 'Monday after Whitsun, 3 days' — which is what a
        future reader will want to check against the document. On a Name it is
        the form as printed where the toponym has been normalised; on a
        Geometry, the coordinates as printed ('03-47S/13038E', '??'); on a
        Timespan, the date as written ('about 1841'). On an Attestation it is
        the source's own wording of the relation the attestation asserts
        ('part of Berkshire', 'within Buckingham'), before that relation is
        mapped to a RelationType; an attestation asserts at most one relation,
        so the wording is never ambiguous. Like the qualification properties it
        has no rdfs:domain, so it applies to any facet node or attestation.

Whether the attribution of the evidence to the cited source was
        stated by the source or resolved editorially. Should point to a
        concept in a SKOS concept scheme. The starter concepts are:

        - plato:AttributionStated: the source is named where the form
          occurs. The default, and usually omitted.
        - plato:AttributionInferred: the source was given as 'ibidem' or
          'idem' and resolved by an editor, so the attribution is inferred
          rather than stated. Not marginal: about one attestation in twenty
          in the English Place-Name Society corpus.

        A statement about the citation, not about the form, which is why it
        lives here and not in plato:occurrence_context.

Links an Attestation to a Type classification it assigns to the SpatialEntity.
        An attestation may assert multiple types or no type at all.

Organizational affiliation of the contributor. Links to a
        plato:Organization entity, which can be further described using
        FOAF, schema.org, or other ontology properties. Organizations
        should ideally use persistent identifiers (ROR, ISNI, etc.).

        For simple cases, use contributor_affiliation_string for free-text
        affiliation names.

Links a Gazetteer to a RelationType it declares for its own use: a
        project's 'flows into', with its label, inverse label and the starter
        type it narrows (plato:broader_relation). The JSON profiles carry
        these in a document-level relationTypes array, beside dataSets. A
        relation type PLATO declares needs no declaration here.

The value, where it is a literal: a number, a string, a date. Use
        plato:value_json instead where the value is structured.

What the name denotes. The list is open: 'toponym' (place name),
        'chrononym' (period or era name), 'ethnonym' (people or ethnic
        group), 'demonym' (inhabitants), 'odonym' (street or road name) and
        'hydronym' (water body) are the starter values, and a project may
        add others ('oronym', 'hagionym') provided it documents them in its
        gazetteer metadata. Multiple types are possible (a name that
        functions as both toponym and ethnonym). plato.schema.json carries
        the same open list; earlier releases closed it there, and the two
        serialisations now agree.

        This classifies the referent, not the status of the form. Whether a
        string is an attested spelling, an editorial headword or a derived
        search form is a property of the attestation (plato:form_status),
        because the same string can have a different status in different
        attestations.

Links an Attestation to the Authority (typically a Source or Dataset)
        that grounds it. This provides the provenance chain for the attestation.

        Semantically equivalent to PROV-O's prov:wasDerivedFrom, indicating the
        authority is the origin of the attested knowledge. We don't use formal
        rdfs:subPropertyOf to avoid importing PROV-O's domain/range constraints
        which conflict with PLATO's class structure.

        This is the direct form. Where the citation itself has something to
        say (a page or folio, an attribution resolved from 'ibidem'), use
        plato:has_citation to a Citation node that cites the Authority.
        sourced_by is declared as the property chain has_citation o cites, so
        a reasoner derives it from a Citation; data intended for consumers
        without a reasoner should assert it directly as well.

Well-Known Text representation of the geometry, following OGC/ISO
        standards. Used for GeoSPARQL queries and RDF serialization.
        Supports Point, LineString, Polygon, MultiPoint, MultiLineString,
        MultiPolygon.

Link to a PeriodO period definition (https://perio.do/). When a timespan
        corresponds to a standardized period in PeriodO, this property enables
        alignment and allows PLATO to inherit PeriodO's temporal bounds, spatial
        coverage, and cultural context. Example: 'https://n2t.net/ark:/99152/p06v8w4rb38'

Whose identifier plato:entity_identifier is (e.g. 'geonames', 'wikidata',
        'tgn', 'osm', 'pleiades', 'whg', or the contributing project's own short
        name). Authority-sourced SpatialEntities carry their origin namespace;
        contributed SpatialEntities that cannot be linked to any authority
        receive the 'whg' namespace.

Links a facet node to its anchor entity, indicating that this
        facet is defined relationally rather than absolutely. The anchor
        is typically a SpatialEntity, Period, or another facet (Name, Timespan, etc.).

        Common patterns:
        - Spatial relativity: "20km east of Nanjing" (anchor is a SpatialEntity)
        - Temporal relativity: "during the reign of Justinian" (anchor is a Period)
        - Name relativity: "also known as Rome" (anchor is another Name)

        A facet may have more than one anchor where its qualifier needs them:
        "between the 5th cataract and Meroe" is plato:BetweenXAndY with
        exactly two values of relative_to, in no particular order. A bearing
        or a distance (plato:relative_bearing, plato:relative_distance) is
        measured from one point, so a facet that has either has exactly one
        anchor. A location given relative to several places at once ("in the
        territory of Theadelpheia, Euhemeria and Philoteris") is several
        attestations, a containment or a nearness for each place, not one
        facet with many anchors.
Links a Gazetteer to a GazetteerGroup.

Role of the contributor in the project or gazetteer. Examples:
        'principal_investigator', 'data_curator', 'student_researcher',
        'automated_process', 'external_contributor'. Helps understand the
        context and authority of contributions.
Links a Source to its parent Dataset.

The more general RelationType of which this one is a narrower case:
        a project's 'flows into' has broader_relation plato:LeadsTo, so any
        attestation of the one is also, for a consumer that follows this
        link, an attestation of the other. A narrower type keeps the
        direction of its broader one. Transitive in use: a consumer should
        follow the chain to the starter type it knows.
Links a Gazetteer to an Attestation contributed within it.
Human-readable label for this type.

A name for the target of plato:relates_to, for display: 'the Buddha',
        'denarius of Hadrian, BM 1872,0709.470'. It belongs on the attestation
        rather than on the target, because the target may be someone else's
        IRI, about which this dataset makes no other statement, and a platform
        showing a place cannot reliably look up every IRI it links to. Give it
        whenever the target is not a SpatialEntity in the same dataset; it is
        harmless, but redundant, when the target is. It names the target; the
        source's own wording of the relation is plato:source_label.

        It may also stand alone, with no plato:relates_to, when the source
        names a target there is nothing to point at (see plato:relates_to).

Free-text explanation of the certainty assessment: quality of
        evidence, degree of scholarly consensus, reliability of source
        (e.g. 'manuscript partially illegible', 'coordinates extrapolated
        from itinerary distances'). Applies wherever certainty does.

The semantic strength of the identity assertion:
        'exactMatch'  — the two SpatialEntities are unambiguously the same entity.
        'closeMatch'  — the two SpatialEntities are believed to be the same entity
                        but with some residual ambiguity (e.g. differing
                        granularity, overlapping but not identical scope).
        'related'     — the two SpatialEntities are closely associated but may not
                        be strictly identical (e.g. a settlement and its
                        administrative district, or successive phases of
                        a site that might or might not constitute continuity).
        'unspecified' — the source links the two but does not say how strongly;
                        honest where the alternative is to guess a strength.

Free-text explanation of the evidence or reasoning supporting
        this identity assertion (e.g. 'coordinates within 500m and
        name forms are cognate', 'identified by contributor during
        reconciliation review', 'confirmed via TGN cross-reference').

Links a CandidateSet to the Gazetteer whose SpatialEntities matches
        were sought for: the dataset its Candidates' sources normally belong
        to, and whose identity relations answer them. A dataset may name its
        candidate sets from its own side (in JSON, the gazetteer's
        candidateSets, which maps to the reverse of this property); no
        inverse property is defined, and both ends should agree.

Where in the cited work the evidence sits: 'p. 412', 'f. 12v', 'Table
        VI, col. 3, row 88', 's.v. Athlone', 'no. xix'. An uninterpreted
        string, deliberately: sources locate themselves inconsistently, and
        normalising the value would destroy exactly the information it is
        there to carry. The same position and shape as PeriodO's source
        locator.

        A property of this citation, not of the source: one Source for a
        printed gazetteer, a different locator on each attestation drawn
        from it. Not to be confused with the spatial sense of 'locator' in
        the plato:geometry_role comment, a proxy point standing in for an
        entity.

Links a meta-Attestation to the Attestation it comments on or relates to.
        Used with plato:has_meta_type to specify the nature of the relationship.
        A meta-attestation need not carry plato:attests_about: it is about its
        target, and through it about the target's SpatialEntity. Where it does
        carry one (as when nested under a place in place-centric JSON), that
        should be the target's.

        Example: A meta-attestation might assert that one source's geometry
        attestation contradicts another source's geometry attestation for the
        same SpatialEntity.

ISO 15924 script code (e.g., 'Arab' for Arabic script, 'Latn' for
        Latin script, 'Hant' for Traditional Han characters). Important for
        names that may appear in multiple scripts.

A structured value serialised as JSON, whose shape is declared by
        plato:value_type. Use plato:value_literal instead for scalar values.

Links an IdentityRelation to the Candidate it was made in response to,
        preserving the algorithmic provenance. The answer may be yes or no: a
        relation bundled by an Attestation marked plato:negated may point at the
        Candidate it denies, as one in an accepting Attestation points at the
        Candidate it accepts, so that a rejection is recorded, attributed and
        dated like an acceptance. Its subject and object should be the Candidate's
        source and candidate, in either order. Several relations, in different
        attestations, may point at one Candidate (it was accepted, withdrawn and
        accepted again, or two reviewers answered it); none of them changes it.
        The Candidate is published in a CandidateSet, which should be published
        wherever the dataset citing it is; a validator that has the set should
        warn when promoted_from names no Candidate in it. Optional: identity
        relations can also be asserted directly, without a prior Candidate.

What this geometry depicts, as distinct from how precisely it is known
        (plato:spatial_precision) or where its indexing point falls
        (plato:repr_point). A SpatialEntity may be attested with several geometries at
        once — a built extent, the location of a specific central feature, a
        proxy standing in for the whole, the anchor of a map label — and without
        a declared role a consumer cannot tell them apart, nor state which one
        an analysis used.

        Should point to a concept in a SKOS concept scheme (e.g. plato:Extent,
        plato:FeaturePoint, plato:RepresentativePoint, plato:LabelAnchor,
        plato:Itinerary). Using URIs rather than free text lets gazetteers that
        record geometry differently be compared.

        Note that role is orthogonal to precision: a proxy locator may be
        surveyed to the metre and still not depict the SpatialEntity it stands for. A
        parish church's coordinates contributed as a locator for a town are a
        representative point of high precision, not an imprecise feature point.

The name of the contributor (person, team, or automated process).
        For persons, should be the full name as preferred by the contributor.
        For teams, the team name. For automated processes, a descriptive name.

The Authority (Source or Dataset) that provides evidence for
        this identity assertion, if any.

Confidence in the identity assertion, from 0.0 to 1.0. This is
        the epistemic certainty of the asserter, distinct from identity_type
        which describes the semantic nature of the relationship.
        A closeMatch can have high certainty ('I'm confident these are
        close but not exact') and an exactMatch can have low certainty
        ('I think they're identical but I'm not sure').

        Any XSD numeric datatype is accepted, from 0 to 1 (xsd:decimal, xsd:double,
        xsd:float, xsd:integer and the others), so it has no rdfs:range.
        PLATO tools writes a whole number as xsd:integer and any other as
        xsd:double, as JSON-LD does.

True when the source states that what this attestation bundles is not
        so: that a place had no market, that a name was not used, that a grant
        was refused. The attestation is still about a real SpatialEntity (the
        town that had no market), with the facet the source denies (a Type
        'market'); nothing that never existed need be invented. A denial is a
        statement a source makes, often a certain one, so it is neither low
        certainty nor a meta-attestation, which needs a claim to contradict.
        The 1886 return of market rights answered for every borough and
        district in England and Wales, and 1,000 of its 1,813 rows are denials.

        A consumer that does not implement this property will read a denial
        as an assertion, the opposite of what the source says. So it must be
        honoured: a tool that cannot express a denial in its target format
        must leave the attestation out and report it, never write it as an
        assertion. Bundle one denied facet per attestation, so that what is
        denied is never in doubt. Absent or false, the attestation asserts.
The agent who made or confirmed this identity assertion.

Numeric precision indicator in years. For example, a decade-level
        precision would have value 10, century-level would be 100. Enables
        computational comparison of precision across timespans.

Whether a transcribed value is whole: a concept in
        plato:TranscriptionCompletenessScheme, plato:TranscriptionComplete,
        plato:TranscriptionReconstructable (part is lost but can be supplied
        with confidence) or plato:TranscriptionNonReconstructable (part is lost
        and cannot be supplied). A different axis from accuracy: a damaged form
        can be accurately read as far as it goes. No rdfs:domain, as for
        accuracy.

How long the timespan lasted, as an xsd:duration ('P42D' for six
        weeks, 'P1D' for a day), where the source states a length: a stay at
        a stop on an itinerary, a siege, a fair. It may stand alone, when the
        source gives a length and no dates, or beside the bounds, which it
        does not replace. xsd:duration has no weeks, so weeks are written as
        days; the source's own words ('staid 6 weekes') are
        plato:source_label on the same timespan.

Epistemic certainty, from 0.0 (completely uncertain) to 1.0
        (completely certain). On an Attestation it is the contributor's
        confidence in the bundle as a whole. On a facet node (Name, Geometry,
        Timespan, Type, PropertyValue) it is the confidence in that value
        alone, and may differ from the attestation's overall certainty.
        Certainty reflects the limits of evidence: better evidence could in
        principle raise it. Distinct from fuzziness (the referent has no
        sharp boundary) and from spatial_precision (how finely a location
        is specified). No rdfs:domain, so it can qualify any node.

        It is never the source's own confidence: how firmly a source asserts
        what it says (hedging, hearsay, doubt) is plato:source_stance.

        Any XSD numeric datatype is accepted, from 0 to 1 (xsd:decimal, xsd:double,
        xsd:float, xsd:integer and the others), so it has no rdfs:range.
        PLATO tools writes a whole number as xsd:integer and any other as
        xsd:double, as JSON-LD does.

The Authority (a Source or a Dataset) this Citation uses. Exactly one
        per Citation: an attestation resting on two sources has two
        Citations.
The first SpatialEntity in an identity assertion.

Links a Period authority to its temporal extent, represented as a
        Timespan node. Used for locally-defined periods or when more detailed
        temporal modeling is needed than provided by external period definitions.

Convex hull of the geometry as WKT Polygon. Used for quick spatial
        filtering before more expensive exact geometry operations. Optional
        but recommended for complex geometries.

URI declaring the shape of a structured value, so that a consumer can
        tell whether it understands the value before attempting to read it.
        Omitted for literal values.

        Not every attribute a source states is scalar. A market's trading day
        — 'the Monday after Whitsun, for three days' — is a recurrence rule
        anchored to a moveable feast, and flattening it to a string would
        reproduce the loss this class exists to prevent. The ontology stays
        agnostic about such shapes: it records which shape is in use and
        leaves the definition to the vocabulary that owns it.

Free-text notes providing additional context about this attestation.
        Can include transcriptions, translations, editorial comments, or
        other information that doesn't fit structured fields.

Precision qualifier for this geometry: 'exact' (surveyed or GPS),
        'approximate' (estimated from maps or descriptions), 'uncertain'
        (multiple possible locations), 'historical_approximate' (based on
        historical sources with inherent imprecision). Multiple values
        possible for heterogeneous geometries.
Datatype of the literal value (e.g. xsd:integer, xsd:decimal, xsd:string).

Links a Gazetteer to an IdentityRelation asserted within it. The
        submission profiles carry identity relations at the top level of a
        document, beside the entities and attestations, and this is the
        property that top level maps to.

The earliest possible end date for this timespan. Together with
        end_latest, defines the uncertainty range for when the interval ended.
        May be null for unknown or deliberately open-end intervals.

A single representative point (centroid, label point, or best
        estimate) for spatial indexing and distance queries. Stored as WKT
        Point. Required for all geometries to enable spatial search.

The earliest possible start date for this timespan. Together with
        start_latest, defines the uncertainty range for when the interval began.
        Use ISO 8601 format (e.g., '1453-05-29') or a year of at least four
        digits ('0921', '-12000') for year-level precision; deep-time years
        have as many digits as they need, as in xsd:gYear. May be null for unknown or deliberately
        open-beginning intervals.

        The range is rdfs:Literal rather than a single datatype, because one
        property carries values of three shapes. A plain string is conformant;
        a producer that can type by shape should emit xsd:gYear for a year,
        xsd:date for a day and xsd:dateTime otherwise, so that a store can
        index and compare the bounds. The same applies to start_latest,
        end_earliest and end_latest.

Boolean flag indicating that the start of this interval is deliberately
        unspecified (not merely unknown). True for intervals like 'everything
        before 1453' or 'prehistory until...'. Distinct from null start_earliest,
        which indicates unknown start. Aligns with PeriodO's OpenBeginningInterval.

The agent (person, team, or process) who created this attestation.

        Semantically equivalent to PROV-O's prov:wasAttributedTo for provenance
        tracking. We don't use formal rdfs:subPropertyOf to avoid importing
        PROV-O's domain/range constraints. Distinct from sourced_by, which
        indicates the historical source being cited.

BCP 47 language tag for this name (e.g., 'ar' for Arabic, 'zh-Hans'
        for Simplified Chinese). Recommended: use ISO 639-3 three-letter codes
        within BCP 47 for better granularity (e.g., 'ara', 'cmn').

What this attestation's timespans date: a concept in
        plato:TimespanRoleScheme. plato:WhenTrue, the default and usually
        omitted, is the period during which what the attestation bundles held,
        according to the source (see plato:attests_timespan).
        plato:EvidenceSpan is the span of the evidence: the dates of the
        earliest and latest documents that mention the entity, as many
        gazetteers date a place (Trismegistos Places, for one). It does not say
        that the entity existed, or bore any name, throughout.

        It is on the attestation, not the Timespan, because a Timespan is a
        reusable node that other attestations may share, and the role of a
        date belongs to the claim that uses it. An attestation window is one
        attestation about the place that carries the timespan and nothing
        else, with this role; it is never repeated on each name. Where the
        attestations of the evidence are themselves in the data, the window
        can be worked out from their dates, and is then plato:computed. A
        consumer that cannot express an EvidenceSpan must report it as a
        loss, and must not show the window as the dates of the place.

Boolean flag indicating that the end of this interval is deliberately
        unspecified (not merely unknown). True for ongoing periods like 'Modern
        era (1800-present)' or situations where the end does not exist. Aligns
        with PeriodO's OpenEndInterval.
Publication status: 'draft' or 'published'. From 'published' on, the Gazetteer's attestations are append-only (see plato:Gazetteer).
Inverse label (e.g. 'has_capital').

A formatted citation string for this source or other authority. The
        domain is Authority, not Source, because any authority can be cited
        formally, a dataset as much as a document. Restricting it to Source
        made a cited Dataset a Source as well, which the disjoint union of
        Authority forbids.

Contact email address for the contributor. Useful for collaboration
        and correspondence about contributed data.

URI of the unit of measurement, where the value has one — a QUDT unit
        or a Wikidata unit item. Omitted for counts and dimensionless values.

GeoJSON representation of the geometry. Used for web mapping
        applications and LPF export. Should be a valid GeoJSON geometry
        object (not a Feature or FeatureCollection). Its datatype is
        rdf:JSON, the JSON literal of JSON-LD 1.1: the JSON-LD context
        maps the geojson key with @type @json, which is the only way a
        GeoJSON object in a document can become a literal rather than
        a node, so every converted dataset already carries rdf:JSON.
        (Before 0.7.0 the range was given as xsd:string, which no
        conversion produced.)

Free-text explanation of the nature of ontological fuzziness
        (e.g. 'regional boundary was never formally demarcated',
        'name used inconsistently across contemporary sources',
        'transition was gradual rather than a discrete event').

Compass bearing from the anchor, in degrees (0–360).
        Primarily used for relative geometries: '90' means east of
        the anchor. May carry its own certainty or fuzziness. Only on a
        facet with exactly one anchor (see plato:relative_to).

        Any XSD numeric datatype is accepted, from 0 to 360 (xsd:decimal, xsd:double,
        xsd:float, xsd:integer and the others), so it has no rdfs:range.
        PLATO tools writes a whole number as xsd:integer and any other as
        xsd:double, as JSON-LD does.
Links a Gazetteer to a SpatialEntity it defines. A SpatialEntity defined elsewhere that this Gazetteer only attests evidence about is not contained in it.

Links a CandidateSet to a Candidate it publishes. The candidate set
        profile carries these in its top-level candidates array, and this is
        the property that array maps to.

The settings that produced the Candidate's score, as text (JSON
        suggested, written in the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (RFC 8785), so
        that the same settings are always the same text, since the text is
        hashed into the Candidate's IRI): a threshold, the weights given to name, place and type,
        the reference sources searched. With plato:algorithm_version it lets
        a score be reproduced or explained. Optional; its form is the
        software's own, since it describes a run of that software rather
        than making a claim about places.
Forward label for the relationship (e.g. 'capital_of').

Links an Attestation to a Citation: its qualified use of one
        Authority, with a locator and an attribution status. An attestation
        may have several, one per source it rests on.

Geographic or cultural region to which this period applies.
        Free text or URI to a place/region. Useful because periods like
        'Medieval' have different temporal bounds in different regions.

The name as the source gives it, in its original script where that is
        known and can be written; otherwise in a scholarly transliteration,
        with plato:script giving the script of the transliteration (usually
        Latn) and plato:transliteration_system saying which system it follows.
        A Demotic name known only in Egyptological transliteration is a
        toponym, not a romanised form: plato:romanized is a further form for
        searching or display, beside a toponym in another script. This is the
        primary property of a Name entity. Required for all Name instances.

Original coordinate reference system. Typically 'EPSG:4326' (WGS84),
        but may reference historical or custom CRS identifiers for historical
        maps. Enables proper interpretation of coordinate values.

The latest possible start date for this timespan. For certain dates,
        this equals start_earliest. For uncertain dates, defines the end of
        the uncertainty range for when the interval began.

Distance from the anchor, in metres. Primarily used for
        relative geometries. May carry its own certainty or fuzziness. Only on
        a facet with exactly one anchor (see plato:relative_to).

        Any XSD numeric datatype is accepted, zero or more (xsd:decimal, xsd:double,
        xsd:float, xsd:integer and the others), so it has no rdfs:range.
        PLATO tools writes a whole number as xsd:integer and any other as
        xsd:double, as JSON-LD does.

The latest possible end date for this timespan. For certain dates,
        this equals end_earliest. For uncertain dates, defines the end of
        the uncertainty range for when the interval ended.
Valid subject type for this relation.

Vector embedding for phonetic similarity search: a vector generated
        from the name's phonetic form, enabling fuzzy matching and
        transliteration-variant detection. Its model and dimension are the
        producer's (WHG v4 uses Symphonym embeddings), so both must be
        stated in the gazetteer's description: vectors from different
        models cannot be compared.

Why the source is cited: as the evidence for the attestation, as a
        source of its data, as related reading, and so on. The value is a
        property of CiTO, the Citation Typing Ontology
        (http://purl.org/spar/cito/): cito:citesAsEvidence,
        cito:citesAsDataSource, cito:citesAsRelated, cito:citesForInformation,
        cito:citesAsRecommendedReading, or another of the properties below
        cito:cites. Only CiTO properties are used, so that every consumer reads
        the same function the same way; a project whose own vocabulary has
        other terms maps them to CiTO when it organises its data.

        Without it, 'this source is the evidence' and 'see this source for
        more' are the same link, which is the distinction an attestation model
        exists to make: 143,418 of Pleiades' 244,759 references are 'see
        further', and only 21,652 are cited as evidence. Absent, the function
        is unstated, as before; a consumer should not assume evidence.

        Only a property CiTO defines is a valid value. An IRI in the CiTO
        namespace is not enough: Pleiades writes cito:seeFurther and
        cito:seeAlso, which CiTO does not define, so the JSON Schema and the
        tables list the accepted properties exactly.

Temporal granularity of the end bound. Values: 'day', 'month',
        'year', 'decade', 'century', 'era', 'geological_period'.

The figure this figure is a part or share of: its denominator, where
        the source defines one. Asserted only from the source, never inferred
        from labels or sums: in Vision of Ireland three of seven plausible
        denominators by name are wrong. The occupied beside the
        total of the same row, or Vision of Ireland's Total Population cube as
        the universe of the others for the same unit and year. RDF Data Cube
        has no such property, and without it which number is the denominator
        of which is lost, unrecoverably once the table is gone.

The nature of a meta-attestation's relationship to its target attestation.
        Should reference a controlled vocabulary concept defining the relationship
        type. The starter concepts, declared in this ontology's MetaTypeScheme:

        - plato:Contradicts: asserts the target attestation is incorrect
        - plato:Supports: provides additional evidence for the target attestation
        - plato:Supersedes: replaces the target attestation with newer information
        - plato:Refines: provides more precise information than the target
        - plato:Challenges: questions the target attestation's validity
        - plato:Bundles: groups the target with other related attestations
        - plato:DerivedFrom: this attestation's value was derived from the
          target's (a normalised search form from an attested spelling)
        - plato:Annotates: adds a remark about the target, with its own source,
          without supporting, contradicting or refining it; the remark is the
          meta-attestation's notes
        - plato:AlternativeTo: this attestation and the target are alternative
          readings of the same evidence, at most one of them right
        - plato:Retracts: the target attestation is withdrawn by whoever made
          it, and kept only so that earlier states can be reproduced

        Using SKOS concepts rather than strings enables vocabulary management
        and multilingual labels.

A controlled-vocabulary term describing the relative relationship
        when bearing and distance are not applicable or not sufficient.
        Should point to a concept in a SKOS concept scheme (e.g.
        plato:Near, plato:Within, plato:Beyond, plato:UpstreamOf,
        plato:BetweenXAndY, plato:DuringReignOf, plato:VariantOf).
        Using URIs rather than free text enables machine reconciliation
        across gazetteers that describe relativity differently.

Links an Attestation to a Name it asserts for the SpatialEntity. An attestation
        may assert multiple names (e.g., primary name and variants) or no name
        at all (e.g., geometry-only attestations).

Specifies the semantic type of a entity-to-entity relationship
        attested by an Attestation. References a RelationType authority
        which defines the relationship's label, inverse, and domain/range
        constraints. Examples: 'capital_of', 'successor_to',
        'connected_by_trade_route_to'.

        The extensible vocabulary pattern allows new relationship types to
        be added as Authority records without modifying the ontology.

This Source is a copy, transcript, edition, calendar or confirmation
        of that one, or a work made from it. A later cartulary copy of a
        charter, an inspeximus, or a printed edition of a manuscript is a
        Source of its own, with its own source_timespan, derived_from the
        document it transmits. An attestation should cite the Source it was
        actually read in; the chain of derived_from links records what that
        Source transmits. A work made from a source, which transmits none of
        it as evidence, is derived_from it too: a count a project takes from
        a register (see plato:computed), or the georeference of a map (see
        plato:Geometry). How it is cited says which it is: a copy is cited as
        the evidence, a georeference as the method used. The kind of
        derivation (copy, edition, calendar, inspeximus, analysis) is not yet
        distinguished; a sub-property or a small vocabulary can be added when
        a project needs it.

Links an Attestation to an IdentityRelation it asserts, so that
        identity relations asserted in one act share its provenance: accepting
        a cluster of n records is one attestation bundling the n-1 exactMatch
        relations of the matches actually made, with the person, the time and
        the cluster's definition as its source. Retracting or superseding the
        attestation withdraws or amends them together. With plato:negated,
        bundling one exactMatch relation, it says the two entities are not the
        same. Closure may be taken within one such attestation only (see
        plato:IdentityRelation). An IdentityRelation's own identity_asserted_by
        and identity_sourced_by remain for one asserted on its own.

Links an Attestation to a PropertyValue it asserts of the SpatialEntity — a
        population, a valuation, an elevation, a market's trading day. An
        attestation may assert several properties or none.

        These are among the commonest things a source says about an entity, and
        they carry exactly the provenance and temporal scoping the attestation
        pattern exists to handle: a population figure is a claim, by a named
        source, about one SpatialEntity, over a Timespan, with a certainty. The
        attestation's own timespans scope the property as they scope every
        other facet in the bundle.

The matching algorithm's score for this candidate, on the scale
        that algorithm uses (named by algorithm_version): higher is more
        similar. It is not a certainty, since a Candidate asserts nothing.

        Any XSD numeric datatype is accepted (xsd:decimal, xsd:double,
        xsd:float, xsd:integer and the others), so it has no rdfs:range.
        PLATO tools writes a whole number as xsd:integer and any other as
        xsd:double, as JSON-LD does.

Links an Attestation to the Timespan during which the attested
        properties (name, geometry, type) were applicable. Distinct from
        the attestation's creation date: this is the historical timespan
        being asserted, not when the assertion was made. It is no wider than
        the source can witness: a source that shows a name in use only in its
        own day (a letter, a survey, a gazetteer consulted now) supports a
        timespan of that day, so the attested timespan then coincides with
        the source's own date (plato:source_timespan), while remaining the
        claim's. Unless plato:timespan_role says otherwise (plato:EvidenceSpan,
        the span of the evidence), the timespan dates what the attestation
        records.
Valid object type for this relation.

How faithfully a transcribed value (a name form, most often) renders
        what the source shows: a concept in plato:TranscriptionAccuracyScheme,
        plato:TranscriptionAccurate, plato:TranscriptionInaccurate or
        plato:TranscriptionFalse. It judges the reading, not the source and not
        the identification: plato:form_status says how a form came to be, and
        plato:certainty how sure anyone is of the attestation, and neither says
        how well the form was read. Pleiades records it for every name.

        Like the other qualification properties it has no rdfs:domain, so a
        transcribed coordinate or date can be judged the same way.

Links an Attestation to the SpatialEntity it is about. Every attestation must
        have exactly one subject entity. This is the primary entity being
        described by the bundled name, geometry, timespan, and type assertions.

        Functional property: each attestation has exactly one subject entity.

The position of a member in an ordered whole, as one source gives it:
        a station on a route, a stop on an itinerary, a segment of a road.
        It sits on the attestation about the member, which relates_to the
        route, itinerary or network with plato:MemberOf; the relates_to target
        is what the number orders, so one place can hold different positions
        on different routes. Lower numbers come first.

        Two members with the same number are alternatives at that point (two
        branches of a road); a source that disagrees with another about the
        order is recorded as its own attestations, with a meta-attestation
        where a judgement is made between them. A member with no sequence is
        in an order the source does not give. The members of an itinerary
        carry their own timespans, from arrival to departure, and the order of
        a journey known only from its dates may be left to those timespans.

The status of the name form this attestation contributes: read in the
        cited source, chosen by the cited authority, or derived by the
        contributing project. Should point to a concept in a SKOS concept
        scheme. The starter concepts are:

        - plato:Attested: a form read in the cited source. The default, and
          usually omitted.
        - plato:Headword: the editorial or preferred form under which the
